It really depends on where you're located. In some places they're considered employees (California had a case over that recently), but in others they're considered contractors. Moreover, because the classifications for "professional" drivers vary state-to-state and country-to-country, where exactly they fall in terms of licensing, taxation etc. is pretty much a toss-up.
Thanks for the reply. Are they at all similar to taxi cavs? Like do they get paid to drive people around?

Basically, yes. Drivers use an app on their phone to track fares (much like a taxi meter) and routes, with payment via a credit card attached to the rider's Uber account. Fares are calculated based on base values for time and distance (again, same as a taxi), which are then multiplied by a factor (locked in when the ride is hailed via the app) that's adjusted by Uber to manage supply and demand (basically, if there are way more people wanting rides than drivers on the road, they keep upping the price until either some of the riders quit or more drivers show up). In some areas they also offer courier parcel delivery, but I think that's pretty limited for now. Some drivers are part-time, some are full-time, and in most places Uber offers several tiers of service based on the vehicle and driver type.

The big difference between an Uber and a taxi is that a taxi can be hailed off the street (or park and wait for fares), whereas an Uber is always dispatched to potential fares via a centralized booking system.
Wow. Again thanks for the reply that sounds like a really crazy field to work in.

They're people who have signed up to drive people when Uber connects them. The people pay Uber for a ride, and Uber passes on most of the fee for the ride to the driver.

Taxi's generally are the only drivers legally allowed to pick up people flagging them down for money, but other drivers have always been able to offer pre-scheduled rides (limos and car services). Uber greatly reduces the time required to pre-schedule a ride, so it's like a car service legally, but offers very taxi like functionality to passengers.

Because Uber handles all the billing and gives them clients, some states consider that an employee and some states do not (the US essentially has 50 copies of rules with slight twists on how they are written or interpreted).
